name: Ori Time Machine
description: Amos Ori's vacuum time machine core of 2005: a plane fronted gravitational wave closed up along one direction, whose circles turn from spacelike to timelike. With $f = a(x^2 - y^2)/2$ causality first fails on a single closed null geodesic, and closed timelike curves fill the region beyond it.
convention: No coordinate carries dimensions of time, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter. The metric fixes no length, so the drawings take any length $\ell$ as their unit and $\ell^2$ as their unit of area, while $L$ is always the period of $z$, as in Ori's paper.
history: Can a time machine be built from ordinary beginnings, an initial state with no closed timelike curves in it [ori2005]? Amos Ori's answer of 2005 is a time machine whose core is made of nothing but a gravitational wave [ori2005]. The core is the vacuum spacetime $ds^2 = dx^2 + dy^2 - 2\,dz\,dT + [f(x, y, z) - T]\,dz^2$, in which $z$ runs round a circle and $f$ is any function harmonic in $x$ and $y$ [ori2005]. Each circle of $z$ starts out as a direction in space and slowly tips over into a direction in time as $T$ grows, spacelike while $T < f$ and timelike once $T > f$ [ori2005]. Nothing breaks along the way: the metric is regular everywhere, with $\det g = -1$, and locally it is a plane fronted wave [ori2005, stephani2003]. With the wave switched off, $f = 0$, the core is flat Misner space carried to four dimensions [ori2005, misner1967].¶Why vacuum? The time machines before it either held their closed timelike curves from the start, as Kurt Gödel's universe does, brought them in from infinity, as J. Richard Gott's cosmic strings do, or needed matter of negative energy density, as the wormhole of Michael Morris, Kip Thorne, and Ulvi Yurtsever does [ori2005, godel1949, gott1991, ori1991, morris1988prl]. Ori's own model of 1993, worked out further with Yoav Soen in 1994 and 1996, avoids all three: its closed timelike curves evolve in a bounded region out of a regular initial slice, and its matter obeys the weak and dominant energy conditions [ori1993, ori1994, soen1996]. That matter fits no known field, so no field equations say how it evolves, and Ori turned to the most elementary field there is, empty space itself [ori2005].¶For a concrete machine Ori chose a simple wave, $f = a(x^2 - y^2)/2$, a linearly polarized plane wave of small amplitude $a$ [ori2005]. He then picked a clock suited to it, $t = T - a(x^2 - y^2)/2 + e(x^2 + y^2)$ with $e > (2e + a)^2$, whose surfaces $t < 0$ are all spacelike, each one a moment of space [ori2005]. At $t = 0$ one circle, the central one at $x = y = 0$, has tipped just far enough to be a light ray: a single closed null geodesic, $N$, where causality first breaks [ori2005]. The circles around it follow, the one at $x$ and $y$ turning timelike once $t > e(x^2 + y^2)$ [ori2005]. Misner space is more fragile: its whole surface $T = 0$ is filled with closed light rays, and an arbitrarily small constant added to $g_{xz}$ or $g_{yz}$ makes them disappear [ori2005]. In the curved core the closed light rays are isolated, as $N$ is, and that instability is gone [ori2005].¶A builder controls only a finite region, and Ori wanted that to be enough: "presumably even an advanced civilization will not be able to control the initial data in the entire space" [ori2005]. So the data that set the machine going sit on a compact piece $S_0$ of an initial surface, inside the core [ori2005]. The region those data determine cannot itself hold a closed causal curve, so the most a builder can ask for is a closed light ray on its edge, and $N$ lies there [ori2005]. Whatever smooth spacetime continues past $N$ contains closed timelike curves, because the circle at $N$ keeps tipping, $\partial_t g_{zz} < 0$ [ori2005].¶Two theorems seem to forbid a machine like this, Frank Tipler's of 1976 and 1977 and Stephen Hawking's of 1992: in a spacetime that obeys the weak energy condition, closed timelike curves cannot be produced in a compact region [olum2000, tipler1976, tipler1977, hawking1992]. Hawking's applies to a compactly generated machine, one whose chronology horizon is made of light rays that, followed back in time, enter a compact region and stay there [hawking1992, ori2005]. Ori's is probably not of that kind, and it passes Tipler's because $N$ is incomplete to the future [ori2005]. Ken Olum's analysis of the Ori-Soen model in 2000 placed its closed light ray where the Cauchy horizon ends, with the causality violation originating outside the region that obeys the weak energy condition [olum2000]. Built from normal matter, he argued, the model might turn singular where the causality violation would otherwise take place [olum2000].¶The whole machine is the core cut off at $x^2 + y^2 = \rho_0^2$, an empty torus, wrapped in a finite region of matter that obeys the weak, dominant, and strong energy conditions, with Schwarzschild's geometry outside [ori2005]. From far away it is an ordinary mass: the model is regular, asymptotically flat, and topologically trivial [ori2005]. The wrapping was still made of no known field, and Ori's second model, of 2007, wraps a different vacuum core in plain dust [ori2005, ori2007]. That core is Schwarzschild's metric with its sphere turned into a hyperbolic plane and its coordinate $t$ made periodic, and its closed light rays fill a whole horizon, as Misner's do [ori2007]. Ori worried there that a singularity might form arbitrarily close to the lone $N$ of the 2005 core, following Olum's argument about the earlier models [ori2007, olum2000].¶The geometry of the 2005 core got a full working over in 2012 from Jurgen Dietz, Alexander Dirmeier, and Mike Scherfner [dietz2012ori]. They found that every geodesic that moves around the circle winds round it infinitely often within a finite affine parameter, so each one is incomplete [dietz2012ori]. Stability "remains the main open question", Ori wrote [ori2005]. Hawking, Sung-Won Kim and Thorne, and Bernard Kay, Marek Radzikowski, and Robert Wald had each found signs that time machines are unstable, classically or to quantum fluctuations, mostly for compactly generated ones [ori2005, hawking1992, kim1991, kay1997]. Ori judged that those signs do not yet rule out building one, and that the answer may have to await a full theory of quantum gravity [ori2005].

related.text: Ori's core with the wave switched off. At $f = 0$ the metric is flat, Misner space with two flat directions beside it [ori2005].
Locally the core is a vacuum pp-wave, and Ori's example is a linearly polarized plane wave. The periodic $z$ is Ori's addition [ori2005].
Two cosmic strings passing at high speed. Ori counted its closed timelike curves as coming from infinity, and built his own to start in a finite region [ori2005, ori1991].
The time machine Morris, Thorne, and Yurtsever made from a wormhole, whose throat needs matter of negative energy density. Ori's model obeys the weak energy condition [ori2005, morris1988prl].
The outside of Ori's full model. Beyond the matter that surrounds the vacuum core, the geometry is Schwarzschild's [ori2005].
Rotating dust with closed timelike curves through every event, there from the start. Ori built his model so that they first appear at a definite moment, inside a finite region [ori2005, godel1949].

coordinates.name: Vacuum Core
domains: T = f \;\text{(the circle of constant } T, x, y \text{ is null)}
T > f \;\text{(the circles of constant } T, x, y \text{ are closed timelike curves)}

parameters.description: Any function periodic in $z$ with period $L$, carrying dimensions of area; the core is a vacuum exactly where it is harmonic in $x$ and $y$, $\partial_x^2 f + \partial_y^2 f = 0$, and flat where it depends on $z$ alone

coordinates.convention: We use Ori's coordinates $(T, x, y, z)$, with $x$ and $y$ lengths, $z$ dimensionless and periodic with period $L$, and $T$ carrying dimensions of area. The function $f$ of $x$, $y$, and $z$ is free, and the core is a vacuum where $\partial_x^2 f + \partial_y^2 f = 0$, as in Ori's example $f = a(x^2 - y^2)/2$ with $a$ a small positive number.

coordinates.name: Spacelike Foliation
domains: x = y = t = 0 \;\text{(the closed null geodesic } N\text{)}
t > e\left(x^2 + y^2\right) \;\text{(the circles of constant } t, x, y \text{ are closed timelike curves)}

parameters.description: Amplitude of the wave in Ori's example $f = a(x^2 - y^2)/2$, a small positive number
Positive number that fixes the surfaces of constant $t$, with $e > a$ and $e > (2e + a)^2$

coordinates.convention: We use Ori's coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$ for the core with $f = a(x^2 - y^2)/2$, where $t = T - a(x^2 - y^2)/2 + e(x^2 + y^2)$ carries dimensions of area, $x$ and $y$ are lengths, and $z$ is dimensionless and periodic with period $L$. The numbers $a$ and $e$ satisfy $0 < a < e$ and $e > (2e + a)^2$, so that every surface of constant $t < 0$ is spacelike.
coordinates.line_element: ds^2 = dx^2 + dy^2 - 2\,dz\,dt + \left(e\left(x^2 + y^2\right) - t\right)dz^2 + 2\left(\left(2e - a\right)x\,dx + \left(2e + a\right)y\,dy\right)dz

coordinates.name: Brinkmann
domains: uv < -a\left(x^2 - y^2\right) \;\text{(the closed curves of constant } uv, x, y \text{ are timelike)}

parameters.description: Amplitude of the wave in Ori's example $f = a(x^2 - y^2)/2$, a small positive number
Period of $z = -2\ln(-u/2)$; a circuit of the closed direction is a boost of rapidity $L/2$

coordinates.convention: We use Brinkmann coordinates $(u, v, x, y)$ for the core with $f = a(x^2 - y^2)/2$, where $u = -2\exp(-z/2)$ is dimensionless and negative, $v = T\exp(z/2)$ carries dimensions of area, and $x$ and $y$ are lengths. A circuit of $z$ is the boost that takes $(u, v)$ to $(u\exp(-L/2), v\exp(L/2))$.
